info.title: Planning lazy stacks for large row lists

parts.text: Lets plan lazy stacks. What do we have so far. What decisions do we need to make? We want something that can handle many thousands of rows without a sweat, ensuring that only the elements visible in the viewport is actaully rendered.

Let me research the codebase for lazy stacks. The AGENTS.md mentions LAZY_VGRID 0x15, LAZY_HGRID 0x16, LAZY_VSTACK 0x1B, LAZY_HSTACK 0x1C as component types. Let me check the specs and implementations.

Let me explore.
I'll research the current state of lazy stacks across the specs and implementations.

### Gauge — `GAUGE` 0x08

A value shown against a scale (SwiftUI `Gauge`).

- **Protocol**: a leaf node with `VALUE` (0x2006), `MIN_VALUE` (0x2007),

---

## B. Layout & Container Primitives

Layout primitives arrange children. They carry `SPACING` (0x0001),
`ALIGNMENT` (0x0002), and `CONTENT_MARGINS` (0x0005), plus layout modifiers from
[MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md#1-layout). Renderers map them to their native
layout primitives.

### The stack layout model

`VStack`/`HStack` (and the lazy stacks) follow the **SwiftUI / Jetpack Compose
layout model**: a stack *proposes* a size to each child, the child reports its
own size, and the stack *places* it. The protocol transmits **intent** — size
kinds and alignment — never geometry; the renderer resolves the proposal with
its native layout engine. The full allocation contract is
[LAYOUT.md](./LAYOUT.md); the essentials:

**Size kinds.** Each `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` is one of three kinds (LAYOUT.md §size
model):

|------|-----------|---------|

| C2 | Fixed `220×220` child | a `280`-wide column, cross axis | exactly `220` on the cross axis, aligned (not filled to `280`) |
| C3 | `Fill`-height container | a `HUG`-height child | the child keeps its natural height; leftover stays empty / goes to a `Fill` sibling |
| C4 | Composite button, no frame | a `Fill`-height column | content height (not absorbed/stretched to the viewport) |
| C5 | Hug `Text` | a stack | natural size on both axes (not stretched cross-axis) |
| C6 | Fixed-width `VStack` | fixed `200` box, taller children | children lay out within `200`; overflow is visible unless `CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it |
| C7 | `Text` `WIDTH=120`, longer content | a column | wraps at word boundaries within `120`; natural height = line count × line height |
| C8 | `Text` long content, `LINE_LIMIT=2` | a `200`-wide column | at most 2 lines; overflow on the last visible line tail-ellipsized (`…`) |
| C9 | `Text` `LINE_LIMIT=1`, `TRUNCATION_MODE=Head` | a `200`-wide column | single line, ellipsis at the start, the tail preserved |

**`ProxyView` (proxy view).** A container whose child subtree is served by
**another** Pathland server — it lets one app compose views from several servers
into a single unified document. It is **not** `children(...)`-bearing: the app
does not author the subtree; the proxying server fetches it from the origin
(blocking `META::RESYNC` at SSR, live deltas over the origin connection),
**remaps its node ids** into a disjoint high range, and splices it in
([PROXY.md](./PROXY.md)). `endpoint` is the origin server's base URL (app-
configured, never client-supplied); `route` is the origin route to render;
`credential` names the service credential the proxying server presents to the
origin. The proxy node lays out as a **transparent passthrough** container
(§[PRIMITIVES.md §ProxyView](./PRIMITIVES.md#proxyview--proxy_view-0x1e)) and
takes size modifiers like any view.

Alignment is **position-only** (SwiftUI/Compose parity): `VStack` takes a
`HorizontalAlignment` (leading/center/trailing), `HStack` a `VerticalAlignment`
(top/center/bottom), and `ZStack`/grids (plus the `frame` modifier's content
alignment) a 2D `Alignment` (topLeading … bottomTrailing). Stretching a child is
its `FILL` size kind, never an alignment.

(SwiftUI `LazyVGrid(columns:)` / Compose `GridCells.Fixed(n)` parity), never
chainable modifiers. The grid's own size uses the universal `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`
frame model — a `Frame` on a grid is a pixel box, never a count. A count is
`int` in the DSL and emits a positive F32; absent = auto-fit. The static `Grid`
takes optional `columns`/`rows` (both absent = SwiftUI `Grid` auto-fit);
`LazyVGrid` takes `columns`; `LazyHGrid` takes `rows`.

**`GridItem` (per-track sizes)**: a **`List<GridItem>`** config value expresses
per-track sizes (SwiftUI `GridItem` / Compose `GridCells` parity) —
`GridItem.flexible()` (`flex`), `GridItem.fixed(pts)` (`fixed:<pts>`),
`GridItem.adaptive(min)` (`adaptive:<min>`). The list serializes to the
`GRID_TRACKS` STRING property (comma-separated), which **takes precedence** over
the counts; a count is the `N`×`flexible` sugar. CSS-grid-native — renderers
without a native per-track equivalent size tracks naturally (renderer status,
spec/PRIMITIVES.md §grid model).

Two-way value controls bind a `WritableSignal` (a config value). Actions bind a
callback. Controls marked **content-bearing** expose `children(...)` for their
content (their style turns it into the control's child, [§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).

| Control | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Kotlin DSL | Emits / Binds |
|---------|---------------------------|----------|---------------|
| `Button` | `Button("title", action)` / `Button(action:label:)` | **content-bearing** — `Button.make(b -> b.title(String).action(Runnable))` and/or `.children(View)`; the title string is handed to the active `ButtonStyle`, an explicit child takes precedence ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)) | `BUTTON` 0x20 (control node); tap = composed `POINTER_DOWN`+`POINTER_UP` |

An AI (or a human) generating a Pathland DSL in a new language MUST produce the
following and verify each item. This is a checklist; the authoritative details
are the companion specs.

### 9.1 Required surface

- [ ] **Views/controls** — every entry of [§4](#4-view-surface):
  `Text`, `Image`, `Color`, `Shape` (all `ShapeKind`s), `Divider`, `Spacer`,
  `ProgressView`, `Gauge`; `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`,
  `ScrollView`,
  `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`; `Button`,
  `TextField`, `SecureField`, `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`,
  `Picker`, `Menu`, `DatePicker`, `ColorPicker`.
- [ ] **The three operations** — configure values, apply modifiers, supply
  children — available at creation or by chaining, in any order
  ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)). Each language maps them to its idiom
  ([§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)).
- [ ] **Modifiers** — every entry of [§5](#5-modifier-surface), applicable to
  any view, innermost-first, emitting one property per underlying argument; a
  modifier's type carries no `Mod` suffix.
- [ ] **Custom modifiers / unified mechanism** — a `ViewModifier` authoring
  surface (`body(content) -> View`) + a chainable `modifiers(...)` operation on
  **any** view; **core modifiers are implemented through the same mechanism**,
  never a separate syntax ([§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)).
- [ ] **Shared config with styles** — a style's `makeBody(Config)` receives the
  same config type the control configured via `make(...)`
  ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
- [ ] **Signals** — `signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`,
  `get`/`set`/`update`/`asReadonly`, with equality suppression, synchronous
  flush, glitch-free propagation, error caching, write discipline, circular
  detection ([§3.1](#31-signal-surface)).

So lazy stacks exist in the protocol surface as component IDs and allocation identical to eager. But the actual realization/windowing isn't implemented anywhere. Let me check implementation status of renderers: HTML, GTK, Qt, TS DOM. Also how would the app transmit many thousands of rows? The DSL creates all children eagerly in Kotlin, which itself is a problem: the app builds thousands of Node objects and the emitter transmits them all. The spec says renderer MAY defer realizing. But to handle thousands of rows "without a sweat", we need:
1. App-side lazy data source (ForEach with a data provider / item count) so the app doesn't build thousands of nodes.
2. Protocol for the renderer to request a window (visible range) — an event from host to guest.
3. Or the app emits all children but the renderer virtualizes (only DOM elements for visible rows). That handles DOM cost but still wire/emitter cost.

Let me look at how ForEach works, events, and whether there's any viewport/scroll event infrastructure. Also look at spec EVENTS for SCROLL/WHEEL and possible "request rows" event.

Let me search for ForEach, scroll events, viewport, "visible".

So currently lazy containers are just treated identically to eager containers. No virtualization at all. Let me check status.md files to confirm "not implemented". Also examine the engine's ForEach and how nodes are emitted, and the wire batch sizes. Let me check docs/decisions/0011 explicit layout allocation maybe relevant. And spec/ENGINE.md for emission model. Also check PROXY maybe not relevant.

Key design questions:
1. Where does virtualization live? The spec currently says "renderer MAY defer realizing off-screen cells... Realization never changes layout". But with the protocol, the renderer cannot invent nodes that weren't transmitted. If the app transmits all children, the renderer can defer DOM/widget creation, but it must know each child's size to position unrendered ones — it doesn't. Alternative: the app is responsible for windowing, renderer reports visible range and app emits only the window. That is the "data source" model. Then "lazy" means the app doesn't instantiate all rows.

Actually the spec's current model assumes the renderer receives all children and can discard realized native elements. But a renderer that hasn't realized a node can't know its size, so scroll extents are unknown. To virtualize correctly you need estimated item sizes or fixed row heights. So decisions needed.

Let me inspect the engine ForEach and Node to see if there's a data-provider concept. Also check how full-snapshot SSR handles huge lists. And whether there's a "window" or "range" property anywhere. Search for "window" "range" "count" "data source" "provider".

# pathland-render-gtk — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 27, 2026

The **GTK4 renderer**: maps opcode frames incrementally onto native GTK widgets
(shared-memory desktop path). Protocol contract: `spec/`. Design-token contract:
`spec/TOKENS.md`.

**Note (2026-09-23):** the toolkit-free decode core (`RenderTree`/`HostNode`,
`apply_frame`, token tables + resolution, `concrete_default_tables`,
`render_tree_from_frame`, `describe`) moved to the shared
`pathland-render-core` crate; this crate now consumes it and keeps the
GTK-specific layers (`tokens.rs` native-theme enrichment, `layout.rs`,
`capi.rs`). `pathland_gtk::RenderTree` etc. remain re-exported for
compatibility.

## Implemented

- **Window metadata**: the GTK window title follows `META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA` `TITLE` (fallback: the run-time title); `DESCRIPTION` maps to the window accessible description.

- **Components → widgets** (`widget_kind`/`build_widget`):
  - `VSTACK`/`HSTACK`/`LAZY_VSTACK`/`LAZY_HSTACK` → `GtkBox` (spacing/alignment/
    padding/content-margins),
  - `PROXY_VIEW` (spec/PROXY.md) → `GtkBox` (a transparent container): the spliced
    (id-remapped) origin subtree lays out in place,
  - `TEXT` → `GtkLabel` (text; `TEXT_STYLE`/`FONT_SIZE`/`FONT_WEIGHT`/
    `FONT_FAMILY`/`FONT_DESIGN`/`COLOR` via a Pango `FontDescription`/
    attributes). `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` renders through Pango **markup**
    (nested spans for the v1 runs + `<a href>` links) because pango 0.20 has
    no link attribute; the plain text stays the fallback,
  - `BUTTON` → `GtkButton` (label; composite body when it has children),
  - `ICON` → `GtkImage` (the canonical `ICON_NAME` maps through this renderer's
    own `gtk_icon_name` map to an Adwaita symbolic icon name; `FONT_SIZE` → pixel size,
    `COLOR` → CSS tint; unmapped names fall back to `image-missing`),
  - `GRID`/`LAZY_VGRID`/`LAZY_HGRID` → `GtkGrid` (row-major cells from child
    index + `WIDTH` column count),
  - `SCROLLVIEW` → `GtkScrolledWindow` (single child),
  - `ZSTACK` → `GtkOverlay`,
  - `SPACER` → expanding box, `IMAGE` → `GtkPicture` (`IMAGE_SOURCE`),
  - `TOGGLE` → `GtkSwitch`/`GtkCheckButton`/`GtkToggleButton` by `TOGGLE_STYLE`
    (`SELECTED` ↔ active),
  - `SLIDER` → `GtkScale` (`VALUE`/`MIN`/`MAX`/`STEP`),
  - `TEXT_FIELD` → `GtkEntry` (`LABEL`/`PROMPT`/`IS_SECURE`),
  - `TEXT_EDITOR` → `GtkTextView` (multi-line),
  - `COLOR` → `GtkDrawingArea` (solid fill), `SHAPE` → `GtkDrawingArea`
    (`SHAPE_KIND`), `DIVIDER` → `GtkSeparator`,
  - `PROGRESS_VIEW` → `GtkProgressBar`/`GtkSpinner`,

# Pathland Engine Semantics

**Status:** Draft
**Wire protocol version:** 1
**Last Updated:** November 1, 2026

`OPCODE.md` defines the 16-byte wire format. `CONFORMANCE.md` defines individual
opcode byte vectors. This document defines the **retained-tree engine behavior**
that produces frames: what gets emitted, in what order, and what must emit
nothing.

The shared trace fixtures live in [`engine-traces/`](./engine-traces/). They are
self-contained PLPL batches (opcodes + frame strings), emitted by the canonical
Rust engine and compared byte-for-byte by the JVM engine test.

---

## 1. Scope

**Decision rationale:** [application-owned state and diff-based emission](../docs/decisions/0003-application-state-and-delta-emission.md)
and [native renderer-owned layout](../docs/decisions/0002-native-declarative-layout.md).

The engine:

- owns the application's retained tree and signal bindings;
- compares the current tree with the last emitted snapshot;
- emits only the `TREE` / `PARAMETER` deltas needed to reach the current tree;
- never computes layout and never emits rectangles.

The renderer owns native elements, layout, styling defaults, and input
recognition.

---

## 2. Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Mount** | First emission of a tree. Emits the complete structure and content. |
| **Snapshot** | A full re-emission of the current tree (`META::RESYNC` / reconnect). |
| **Delta** | Opcodes for nodes that changed since the previous emission. |
| **Frame** | One bounded batch of opcodes plus its string data. |
| **Zero-op** | A recompute that emits no opcodes and produces no new frame. |

A renderer may receive any number of deltas after the initial mount/snapshot.
It must converge to the same rendered tree as a fresh snapshot of the same
retained tree.

---

## 3. Node identity

Node ids are assigned **pre-order**, root first, starting at `1`.

```text
VStack(id=1)
├── Text(id=2)
└── Text(id=3)
```

Rules:

- A frame MUST NOT contain two nodes with the same id.
- Structural reconciliation keeps ids stable for position+type-stable nodes.
- A removed node gets `TREE::DELETE_NODE`.
- A new node gets `TREE::CREATE_NODE`.
- A child relationship is established with `TREE::INSERT_CHILD`.
- `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` nodes keep their **pinned** playback id across subtree
  re-emissions (spec/MEDIA.md).

---

## 4. Canonical mount order

For each node, before its children:

1. `TREE::CREATE_NODE`
2. `TREE::INSERT_CHILD` (when the node has a parent)
3. node properties (`PARAMETER::SET_PROPERTY`, including token/string/list
   properties)
4. node text (exactly one of `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT` or
   `PARAMETER::SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT`) and date (`PARAMETER::SET_DATE`)
5. recurse into children, in child order

The child is attached **before** its own content/properties, so an id-keyed
renderer can create and place the native element before applying content.

The trace fixtures assert this order. Property ordering within a node is
deterministic and follows the engine's stored property order.

---

## 5. Reactive emission

The engine records which nodes read each signal during emission:

- a text binding (`node.text_binding`);
- an attributed-text binding (`node.attributed_binding`);
- a property binding (`node.property_bindings`);
- a string-property binding (`node.string_bindings`).

When a signal changes, only the bound nodes re-emit:

- text → `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT`
- attributed text → `PARAMETER::SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` (zero opcodes when the
  encoded payload is unchanged)
- property → `PARAMETER::SET_PROPERTY`
- string property → `PARAMETER::SET_PROPERTY` with the `STRING` value type

An unrelated signal change emits nothing. A write that does not change the
signal value emits nothing.

### Zero-op recompute

An unchanged tree or unchanged signal MUST emit **zero** opcodes and MUST NOT
produce a new frame. This is the steady-state contract that makes the ring
zero-allocation during idle re-renders.

---

## 6. Structural deltas

When a tree changes structurally:

| Change | Required opcodes |
|--------|------------------|
| Node added | `CREATE_NODE` + `INSERT_CHILD` + node content |
| Node removed | `REMOVE_CHILD` (when parented) + `DELETE_NODE` |
| Child reordered | `MOVE_CHILD` (same node ids) |
| Parent changed | remove from old parent + insert under new parent |

The engine does not resend unchanged subtrees. A structural change that leaves
a descendant identical emits no descendant opcodes.

---

## 7. Fit, media, navigation

These are engine-owned surfaces with the same diff discipline:

- **`SIZE_THAT_FITS`**: only the selected candidate is normally transmitted;
  snapshot/SSR emission may include every candidate for first paint.
  `FIT_CHANGED` re-renders only the fit component.
- **Media**: one non-visual `MEDIA_CONTROLLER` node per controller, stable id;
  registered controllers are pinned as root children (so audio needs no view),
  and a `VIDEO` surface references its controller via `MEDIA_CONTROLLER_ID`.
  Transport changes emit only the changed controller property.
- **Navigation**: a `NavigationContainer` is an ordinary tracked component; a
  route change re-renders only its destination slot.

Detailed wire contracts remain in `PRIMITIVES.md`, `MEDIA.md`, and `DSL.md`.

---

## 8. Shared engine traces

**Decision rationale:** [cross-language conformance through shared data](../docs/decisions/0009-cross-language-conformance.md).

Fixtures live under `spec/engine-traces/<scenario>/<step>.plpl.hex`.

- Each file is one **self-contained PLPL batch** (`FrameCodec` format).
- The hex is lowercase; comments start with `#`.
- The batch includes the opcode list and the exact frame string table.
- The fixture is emitted by the canonical Rust engine and compared byte-for-byte
  by the JVM engine test.

### Current scenarios

| Scenario | Steps | Covers |
|----------|-------|--------|
| `mount_text_stack` | `000-mount` | Create/insert order, `SPACING`, `SET_TEXT` |
| `signal_text_delta` | `000-mount`, `001-set-text` | Mount + text-signal delta only |
| `property_signal_delta` | `000-mount`, `001-set-spacing` | Mount + property-signal delta only |
| `styled_text_mount` | `000-mount` | Property-before-text emission order |
| `structural_add_remove` | `000-mount`, `001-add-child`, `002-remove-child` | Create/insert append, remove+delete |

### Generate

From `lib/rust`:

```bash
cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit
```

### Verify

```bash
cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --check
cd lib/java && mvn -q -pl pathland-view-core -am test -Dtest=EngineTraceTest
```

CI regenerates the fixtures from Rust and fails on drift; the Java reactor runs
`EngineTraceTest` as part of `mvn test`.

### Adding a scenario

1. Add the scenario to `pathland-engine-golden`.
2. Run `--emit` and commit the new fixtures with the behavior change.
3. Add the equivalent scenario to the JVM `EngineTraceTest`.
4. Update the table above.

---

## 9. Not covered yet

The trace set is intentionally small at this stage. Future traces should cover:

- structural insert/remove/move deltas;
- unchanged recompute (zero-op) as a frame-level fixture;
- design-token and string/list property deltas;
- window metadata and theme frames;
- fit-slot selection and snapshot emission;
- media transport changes;
- navigation destination swaps.

state.output:
- **`TEXT_CHANGED`**: the new text is a length-prefixed entry
  (`[u32 byteLength][bytes…]`). Over the **shared-memory ring** the renderer
  bump-allocates it into the host-owned **event arena** and `B` is its absolute
  offset (see OPCODE.md); over the **network** it lives in the batch's string
  section referenced by a *relative* `B` offset — exactly the `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT`
  dual convention. A bare opcode cannot resolve the text; batch-aware decoders
  (`pathland-core-transport`, Java `FrameCodec`, TS `decoder.ts`) resolve it.
  The event is reported on **every** edit, including intermediate edits, not
  only on commit.
- **`FOCUS_CHANGED`**: `B` = 1 gained focus, 0 lost focus. The renderer reports
  it for nodes that declared the `FOCUS` listener bit (bit 5). Focus is what
  routes subsequent `KEY_*` events.
- **`EDITING_CHANGED`**: `B` = 1 editing session began, 0 ended. Reported for
  nodes that declared the `EDITING` listener bit (bit 6).
- **`SUBMIT`**: the user committed the field (Enter). Reported for nodes that
  declared the `SUBMIT` listener bit (bit 7). `B` MAY carry the current text as
  a string-section offset (reserved for future use; 0 today).

### Scroll

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | SwiftUI counterpart |
| --------- | ------- | --- | --- | --- | ------- | --------------------- |
| `SCROLL` | 0x0B | targetId | offsetX (f32) | offsetY (f32) | — | `ScrollView` offset, `onScrollPhaseChange` |
| `WHEEL` | 0x0C | targetId | deltaX (f32) | deltaY (f32) | — | `onScrollWheelEvent` / trackpad |

- **`SCROLL`**: the content offset of a `SCROLLVIEW` (logical points), reported
  for nodes that declared the `SCROLL` listener bit (bit 8). The renderer
  reports the absolute offset after each scroll delta.
- **`WHEEL`**: raw wheel/trackpad deltas (logical points), reported for nodes
  that declared the `WHEEL` listener bit (bit 9). Renderers map native scroll
  deltas onto x/y deltas.

### Navigation

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | SwiftUI counterpart |
| --------- | ------- | --- | --- | --- | ------- | --------------------- |
| `NAVIGATE` | 0x0E | 0 | URL string offset | 0 | `NAVIGATE_URL` (0x0001) | browser back/forward (`popstate`), a deep link, or a native back affordance |

### Media

Media events report a
[`MEDIA_CONTROLLER`](./PRIMITIVES.md#media-controller--media_controller-0x30)'s
playback state back to the app — **`A` = the controller node id**, never a media

The store (`StateStore`) is untyped and platform-neutral (in-memory, Redis,
file, SQLite, LocalStorage, NVS flash). `Component` binds its state delegates to
the session's `PersistentState` before the first `body()` render — no annotation
processor or kapt. Other DSLs must offer equivalent explicit wiring.

### 3.4 Structural reactivity (reactive bodies + slots)

The unit of structural reactivity is the **component**. Each child view rendered
by a parent is a tracked component slot: a signal read during its `body()` /
`renderNode()` re-renders **that component**, and the emitter diffs the fresh
subtree against the retained nodes. Kotlin authors therefore use ordinary control
flow instead of a wrapper type:

| Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Kotlin DSL | Rust DSL | Emits |
|----------------------------|----------|----------|-------|
| `if cond { then } else { else }` in a result builder | plain `if` in `body()`; `View.of(() -> …)` for an inline expression | plain `if`/`match` in `build()` | `TREE` deltas (reconcile) |
| `switch value { case a -> v; default -> d }` | plain `switch` in `body()`; `View.of(() -> switch …)` inline | plain `if`/`match` in `build()` | `TREE` deltas (reconcile) |
| `ForEach(items) { … }` | plain `for`/stream for static lists; `ForEach.of(signal, (item, i) -> …)` for a row-scoped component | plain `for` in `build()` (`ForEach` parity: Phase 2) | `TREE` deltas (reconcile) |

**Kotlin realization** — bare control flow in a component body:

```java
@Override
public View body() {
    if (loading.get()) return Spinner.make();
    if (error.get() != null) return ErrorView.make(error.get());

    var rows = new ArrayList<View>();
    for (var track : tracks.get()) rows.add(TrackRow.make(track));
    return VStack.make().children(rows.toArray(View[]::new));
}
```

`View.of(Supplier<View>)` is the **inline** form (Java has no `if` expression),
---
  (`Reactive<T> { Static(T), Signal(SignalId) }`); the former `Bound` /
  `*.bound` modifier surface is folded into it and **removed**.
- Names are recommendations; semantics
  ([§1](#1-design-principles-dsl-flavored)) are the contract.

#### 9.3.1 Cross-language reactive vocabulary

The **names and semantics** are shared; the syntax is the host language's.
Swift is the canonical SwiftUI-shaped reference. Java spells the non-native
helpers as `View.of` / `ForEach.of`; Kotlin and TypeScript use their native
expression and collection forms; Rust parity is Phase 2.

| Concept | Swift | Java | Kotlin | Rust | TypeScript |
|---------|-------|------|--------|------|------------|
| Component render | `var body: some View` | `View body()` | `View body()` | `fn build(&self)` | `body(props)` |
| Signal read | `count` (`@State`), `signal.value` | `sig.get()` | `sig.value` / `sig()` | `sig.get()` | `sig()` |
| Branch | `if`/`switch` in `@ViewBuilder` | `if`/`switch` in `body()`; `View.of(() -> …)` inline | `if`/`when` expressions | `if`/`match` expressions | ternary / `switch` expressions |

| Children | trailing closure | `.children(a, b)` | `.children(a, b)` / trailing lambda | `.children(vec![a, b])` | `children: [a, b]` |

```swift
struct LibraryView: View {
    let tracks: [Track]
    @Binding var trackIndex: Int

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 8) {

            ForEach(tracks) { track in
                TrackRow(track: track, trackIndex: $trackIndex)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

```java
    ForEach.of(tracks, (track, index) -> TrackRowView.make(r -> r

        .index(index)
        .trackIndex(trackIndex))));
```

- **Use native control flow** where the language has it. `View.of` is the Java

  (component-scoped) list; static lists MAY use streams/`map`/`for` directly.
- **Keep the anchors**: `View`, `Signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `State`,
  `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. These are what make the DSLs
  recognizable; casing and construction follow the host language.

  `BiFunction`; Kotlin/Rust authors may name the lambda parameters.

  is a future protocol/emitter feature, not a syntax difference.

Rules:

- **Use native control flow** where the language has it. `View.of` is the Java
  inline form because Java has no `if` expression; Swift/Kotlin/Rust/TypeScript
  use their own `if`/`switch`/`when`/`match`/ternary forms.
- **Use native iteration for static lists.** `ForEach` is the reactive
  (component-scoped) list; static lists MAY use streams/`map`/`for` directly.
- **Keep the anchors**: `View`, `Signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `State`,
  `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. These are what make the DSLs
  recognizable; casing and construction follow the host language.
- **`(item, index)` order** for `ForEach`, matching JavaScript `map` and Java
  `BiFunction`; Kotlin/Rust authors may name the lambda parameters.
- **No keys yet.** The emitter reconciles by position + type; a keyed `ForEach`
  is a future protocol/emitter feature, not a syntax difference.
- **Gaps**: Rust reactive-body/`ForEach` parity is Phase 2; the TypeScript plan
  currently defers structural reactivity; Swift is not implemented yet. Kotlin is
  implemented by `lib/java/pathland-view-core` (Kotlin-owned views over the engine;
  `Text("…")`, `VStack(spacing = 8) { … }`, `.padding(16)`), with its surface and
  gaps tracked in that module's `status.md`.

# ADR-0011: Explicit Fixed/Fill/Hug allocation rather than implicit stretching

**Status:** Accepted
**Recorded:** 2026-11-12 (extracted existing decision; original date not established)
**Scope:** Cross-renderer allocation semantics

## Context

Native renderer-owned layout still needs shared meanings for size and alignment.
Toolkit defaults differ: CSS flexbox stretches cross-axis children by default,
while the documented SwiftUI/Compose model hugs their content.

## Decision

Use Fixed, Fill, and Hug as the per-axis size model. Absent size means Hug;
alignment positions rather than resizes. Only explicit Fill or the contract's
listed greedy primitives demand extra space. Fixed allocation, content fitting,
and clipping are distinct concerns.

## Rationale

The layout specification deliberately follows SwiftUI/Compose rather than CSS's
implicit stretching. Its rationale records the errors this avoids: fixed images
changing size, Fixed/Hug children growing inside Fill containers, and composite
buttons expanding despite content-sized intent.

## Alternatives

Implicit CSS cross-axis stretching and treating fixed size as a minimum/hint
are explicitly excluded. This is shared allocation semantics, not a decision to
move geometry calculation into the engine.

## Consequences

Renderer adapters must override conflicting native defaults. Greedy exceptions
and bounds must be handled explicitly, not generalized into stretch-everything
behavior. The full allocation rules remain in the layout spec.

## Sources and current contract

- [Size model](../../spec/LAYOUT.md#the-size-model).
- [Container allocation](../../spec/LAYOUT.md#container-allocation-rules).
- [Native layout ownership](0002-native-declarative-layout.md).

I have enough. Let me check the ring buffer default size and node id ranges, and the Kotlin emitter's Node to know what data structures exist. Also check if there is a "pinned" concept and node ids. Let me quickly look at the Node class in Java and the Rust engine node.

Actually the important part for planning is decisions. Let me also verify the "lazy" spec says renderer MAY defer realizing, but there's no mechanism for a renderer to get more children (they're all sent). And app-side virtualization requires a renderer→app signal of visible range + app-side item provider.

Let me check whether there's any concept of "item count" or `ForEach` data. No.

Also, I should check how the SSR HTML renderer handles the whole tree: it renders everything into HTML, so thousands of rows means huge HTML. For SSR, to have only visible rows, server must know viewport height — META::VIEWPORT_HEIGHT exists! That's important: server can know viewport dimensions from environment. But item heights unknown. Could use fixed row height or estimated.

Let me read spec on META::ENVIRONMENT viewport fields. And whether SSR environment is sent before render (in server core). Let me check server core PathlandSession SSR and environment.

Let me check quickly.

parts.text:
Important finding: SCROLL events are decoded but InputDispatcher doesn't route them; and the Kotlin DSL doesn't expose onScroll. So scroll events are "draft" and unimplemented in the app layer. For lazy stacks we need a scroll position feedback loop.

Now let me think through the design space and decisions. Let me also check how `META::VIEWPORT_*` is delivered to app (Environment). In server-core, EnvironmentData has viewport, applied via applyEnvironment. Let's check what Environment provides to views.

Also check the Kotlin Environment class to see if viewport is exposed.

Let me check the Rust engine's signal/host for viewport. Actually focus.

Key design approaches:

**A. Renderer-side virtualization (protocol as-is, all children transmitted)**
- App builds all N rows into retained tree; emitter sends all N (or on mount, all).
- Renderer only creates native elements for visible window.
- Problems:
  - Wire/emitter/memory cost O(N) on mount and structural changes; app still allocates N nodes. "Thousands of rows without a sweat" may be okay for a few thousand but not 100k. Not zero-sweat for 100k.
  - Renderer doesn't know sizes of unrealized children, so can't compute scroll extent/positions. Could use fixed/estimated row height property.
  - Renderer must keep the un-realized children in its model to realize later (it already decodes the full tree into RenderTree/HostNode — that's O(N) memory in the renderer anyway).
  - SSR still emits O(N) HTML unless renderer windows it, but server doesn't know viewport height at first paint unless environment given; even then item heights unknown.
  - The spec's current wording ("renderer MAY defer realizing off-screen cells... MAY discard") implicitly supports this model, but it lacks size estimates.

**B. App-side windowing (data-source model)**
- App declares a lazy container with: total item count, item provider/builder, and (optionally) fixed/estimated item size.
- Renderer reports scroll offset / visible range back to app (new event or reuse SCROLL).
- App emits only the window's children (plus spacer/padding to preserve scroll extent).
- Problems:
  - Needs a spacer-based layout trick or explicit "content inset" so scroll extent reflects all N items. Either the lazy container itself renders virtual extent (renderer knows item count + size), or app emits leading/trailing spacer nodes (e.g. a fixed-height COLOR/SPACER) — awkward and not declarative.
  - App owns data; only it can build a row. This is the only way to avoid O(N) app cost.
  - Needs stable node identity so scrolling doesn't recreate/destroy all rows (keys or index-based ids).
  - Network latency per scroll window (fine, coalesced; renderer shows blank/placeholder briefly).

**C. Hybrid: protocol declares item count + fixed size; renderer windows and requests item content by index**
- The lazy container is a "virtualized data container" that knows total count and an item size (fixed or estimated). The renderer realizes a window and requests the app to materialize rows by index. This is essentially React Native FlatList / SwiftUI lazy semantics: the data source lives in the app, renderer asks for indices.
- Protocol needs a new host→guest event `VISIBLE_RANGE` / `REQUEST_ITEMS(targetId, start, count)` and app responds with TREE deltas for the window.
- Or the app subscribes to scroll events and emits window itself (B).
- For SSR, server can pre-render first window using viewport height from environment, and mark total extent.

Which direction fits Pathland's philosophy?
- "Renderers are dumb (execute commands only)" — renderer-side virtualization requires the renderer to know which children to realize, which is arguably rendering strategy, not app state. Principle 1 says renderer MAY retain its rendered-output tree as cache. Virtualization is a rendering optimization, not app state. So renderer-side is philosophically allowed.
- But "only elements visible in viewport are actually rendered" — with renderer-side, all nodes exist in the decoded model, only native elements are lazily created. Is that "rendered"? Arguably yes.
- However the app still pays O(N) in node tree + emission. The user says "handle many thousands of rows without a sweat" — thousands (not millions). Renderer-side with O(N) app nodes might be acceptable for ~10k, but "without a sweat" suggests we want to avoid O(N) work.

Let me think about the protocol-first minimal change. The protocol is declarative and transmits full child list on mount. To truly scale, we need app-side data source. But the spec explicitly says "Allocation is identical to the eager base with windowed realization only" and "Realization never changes layout — a cell's position is always its row-major index in the full cell list." That assumes full list is known to the renderer. So current spec = renderer-side virtualization.

Decision points to present:
1. **Who owns the window?** Renderer-side (full child list sent, renderer realizes visible subset) vs app-side data source (app sends window; renderer asks for ranges) vs hybrid (renderer requests, app provides).
2. **Item sizing model**: fixed row height (fast, exact scrollbar), app-declared estimated size, or measured-and-cached (requires renderer to measure realized rows). For variable-height rows, need estimation + correction, or fixed-size-only v1.
3. **Protocol surface**: new properties on lazy containers? e.g. `ITEM_COUNT`, `ITEM_EXTENT`, `OVERSCAN`? New event for visible range? Or reuse SCROLL + app windowing?
4. **Identity/keys**: stable item ids for reconciliation so scrolling reuses rows. Current emitter reconciles by position+type and "no keys yet". Need keys or index-stable slots.
5. **Emission cost**: mount with N rows — is full mount allowed (renderer windows) or must app emit only a window? Full snapshot/SSR considerations.
6. **Placeholder/extent strategy**: how to represent off-screen space so scrollbar/scroll extent is correct. Renderer-owned virtual extent (needs count+size) vs app-emitted spacers.
7. **SSR/first paint**: server-side rendering for large lists — window on server using viewport height from environment + fixed item size? Or full HTML (bad). Need decision on no-JS.
8. **Scroll feedback**: SCROLL is draft and not dispatched in JVM app layer; need to finish it (and route to lazy container), or add a dedicated `VISIBLE_RANGE` event.
9. **Native renderer mechanics**: GTK/Qt — use GtkListView/GtkColumnView (model+factory, true recycling) vs GtkBox of realized rows? Qt ListView/Repeater vs ColumnLayout. This is renderer-specific but affects protocol (model-driven lists need item data/count). The existing lazy stacks map to GtkBox/QML ColumnLayout (not virtualized).
10. **Which containers in v1**: LazyVStack/LazyHStack first (most common), grids later? Or all four.
11. **Interaction with Fill propagation / stack layout**: virtualized stacks with fixed/estimated heights vs native layout. Need layout contract for virtual extent.
12. **Invalidation**: data changes (insert/remove) shift indices; window re-request, stable ids.
13. **Accessibility/SEO**: only visible rows in DOM hurts SEO/a11y; full SSR or progressive enhancement decision.
14. **Testing/conformance**: golden vectors for windowing, visible-range events, scroll extent.

Given Pathland's principles and constraints, I think the cleanest scalable design is a **hybrid data-source model**:

- Lazy containers carry an **item count** and a **data window** model.
- The app supplies a builder `(index) -> View` plus `count` (a signal). It does not build all rows.
- The renderer reports the **visible index range** to the app (new host→guest event, e.g. `VISIBLE_RANGE` targetId, firstIndex, lastIndex, or a `SCROLL` event the container listens to).
- The app emits only the window's children, but positions them correctly. To get correct scroll extent and avoid reflow, the protocol needs either:
  - (a) fixed item extent per axis (`ITEM_EXTENT` property, f32 points) — renderer computes total extent = count × extent (+ spacing), positions window at `firstIndex × (extent+spacing)`; app emits rows into a virtual container that places them at index offsets, or

- Alternatively, the renderer owns a virtual extent and the app just emits a window of children plus `FIRST_INDEX` (start index) and `ITEM_COUNT`; the renderer positions the window at `firstIndex * (extent+spacing)` and adds leading/trailing virtual space.

This is essentially SwiftUI LazyVStack semantics but with the data source pulled by the renderer. Actually SwiftUI builds all view values (cheap structs) but lazily realizes; the data is in the app. React Native FlatList passes data + renderItem; it computes window and renders a window of items.

```kotlin
LazyVStack(count = items.size, itemExtent = 56f) { index -> RowView(items[index]) }
```

# Pathland architecture skills

Four repository-local skills operationalize the ADR and traceability conventions.
Their source is `.agents/skills/`; OpenCode discovers that directory directly.
No global installation, config change, network access, or upstream LLP install
is required. Other harnesses can use the same Markdown contracts if they support
that location, or load the files explicitly; discovery varies by harness.

| Skill | Purpose | Changes files? |
|-------|---------|----------------|
| [pathland-orient](../../.agents/skills/pathland-orient/SKILL.md) | Assemble task-specific contracts, rationale, tests, and known gaps | No |
| [pathland-decision](../../.agents/skills/pathland-decision/SKILL.md) | Draft an ADR or proposed supersession using the existing template | Only when drafting files is requested; always Proposed |
| [pathland-review](../../.agents/skills/pathland-review/SKILL.md) | Evaluate an ADR, spec proposal, or architecture-sensitive diff | No |
| [pathland-maintain](../../.agents/skills/pathland-maintain/SKILL.md) | Find drift and propose reference/code/doc/status repairs | No |

## Use

In OpenCode, mention the skill by ID, for example:

- `Use @pathland-orient before changing media controller projection.`
- `Use @pathland-decision to draft an ADR for this proposed transport change.`
- `Use @pathland-review to review docs/decisions/0013-swiftui-shaped-signal-dsl.md.`
- `Use @pathland-maintain to audit media identity, or do a pre-pr check of this diff.`

These are prompts, not shell commands or installed slash commands. Skill
discovery depends on the harness/session; if a newly added skill is not yet
advertised, open a new session or ask the agent to read its `SKILL.md` explicitly.
Agents can select relevant skills from their descriptions. Merely loading a
skill does not authorize unrelated edits, acceptance, delegation, external model
calls, commits, or publication. Plan-mode restrictions still take precedence.

## Ownership and boundaries

The [ADR conventions](README.md) and [traceability policy](traceability.md) own
project policy. Skills provide reusable workflows and output shapes; they must
not invent a second authority for requirements or decision approval. Revise them
alongside policy changes and verify their links remain valid.

The design is inspired by [LLP's skills](https://github.com/ccheever/llp/tree/main/skills),
but these are Pathland-specific workflows, not installed upstream copies. They
use existing specs, historical ADRs, `status.md`, and audit evidence—not numbered
LLP documents, foundation/current overlays, or upstream update receipts.
There is no automatic multi-model review, shipping, or decision-acceptance loop.

## Validation and smoke scenarios

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_*.py'
python3 scripts/check-references.py
```

CI checks skill names/descriptions, expected sections, and Markdown target
paths/anchors alongside reference-checker tests. These are structural checks,
not proof that an agent will follow prose. For a behavioral smoke review:

| Scenario | Expected behavior |
|----------|-------------------|
| Orient to media identity | Find MEDIA spec, ADR-0006, Rust/Kotlin references/tests, and the known ordering gap; make no edits |
| Draft a new ADR | Search existing decisions/history, allocate a safe provisional number, use the template, keep Proposed; don't retire the predecessor |
| Review material authored in the same session | Disclose self-review, cite evidence, do not claim independent approval |
| Audit the Rust surface-first layout | Recheck MEDIA-001 against current code; distinguish its violation from playback test coverage; propose a fix, don't apply it |
| Find a broken source anchor | Report the bad target and likely relevant section; do not silently retarget or redefine the contract |
| Encounter conflicting code and spec | Classify the discrepancy and seek a maintainer decision if intent is uncertain; do not bless code by editing the spec |

These scenarios are evaluation guidance, not a claim that live agent executions
have already passed them.

# Architecture traceability and drift

This workflow connects implementation to the current contract and decision
rationale. A reference identifies what governs code; it is **not a certification
that the code complies**. Specs remain authoritative for requirements, ADRs for
decision history, and per-project `status.md` for implementation coverage.

## Source references

Put a standalone comment near the relevant declaration or implementation block:

```rust
// @ref spec/MEDIA.md#5-structural-swaps-the-motivating-contract [implements]
```

Use a repository-root-relative Markdown path, an optional heading fragment,
a required relation, and an optional short gloss following an em dash:

```text
@ref path/to/document.md#heading [relation] — Short explanation
```

| Relation | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `implements` | Implements the referenced requirement |
| `tests` | Exercises the requirement; does not imply exhaustive coverage |
| `constrained-by` | Shaped by an architectural constraint or decision |
| `explains` | Context, not a claim of implementation |
| `historical` | Deliberate reference to retired guidance, not a current constraint |

Normally code/tests point to a **specific spec section**, and that section links
to its ADR. Link directly to an ADR when the architectural boundary itself is
what matters. Use `historical` only for genuine historical context, not to bypass
updating an implementation's governing reference. Proposed ADRs cannot be
implementation constraints until accepted by a maintainer.

Keep directives in source comments (`//`, `///`, `//!`, block-comment `*`, or
`#`), not string literals. References are human-placed breadcrumbs, not
compiler-enforced attachments. The checker validates standalone directive lines;
it does not parse language syntax or prove which declaration a comment governs.
Use normal Markdown links in documentation. This is Pathland's convention,
inspired by LLP, not compatibility with the upstream LLP skill contracts.

## Adoption and change review

- Prioritize non-obvious invariants, architectural boundaries, and behavior an
  agent might otherwise simplify incorrectly. Do not annotate every function.
- Add accurate references when touching governed code; review scope and target
  meaning, not just whether the path exists.
- Requirement changes include spec updates and behavioral tests. Significant
  architectural changes also propose a new ADR, superseding the prior record
  only after maintainer acceptance.
- Keep references, contract changes, tests, and affected `status.md` updates
  together. Do not mechanically annotate files without reviewing their behavior.
- Existing unreferenced code is a review backlog, not an automatic CI failure.

## Drift resolution

Do not assume the code or the document is right merely because it is newer.
Report the discrepancy before changing the governing decision.

| Finding | Resolution |
|---------|------------|
| Code violates a still-valid contract | Fix the implementation and add a regression test |
| Spec misstates intended behavior | Propose a correction and assess compatibility; do not silently bless the code |
| Architecture intentionally changes | Propose a superseding ADR, then coordinate specs, code, and tests |
| Reference is inaccurate or stale | Repair the reference; investigate whether behavior also drifted |
| Intent is uncertain or documents conflict | Record evidence and request a maintainer decision |
| Requirement lacks adequate tests | Record the coverage gap separately from a demonstrated violation |

A finding records: an identifier, audit date and source revision, governing
spec/ADR, implementation symbols, observed behavior, reproduction or test
evidence, existing coverage, and proposed resolution. Distinguish static review,
executed tests, and hypotheses. Never claim a test ran when it did not.

Store cross-project audit reports under `docs/audits/`. Put unresolved
implementation gaps in affected projects' `status.md`, linking to the report;
the audit is evidence, not a competing implementation-status system. Resolve
findings explicitly with a linked fix or a maintainer-approved contract change.
An audit is a dated snapshot, not an automatically current conformance claim.

that the code complies**. Specs remain authoritative for requirements, ADRs for
decision history, and per-project `status.md` for implementation coverage.

## Source references

Put a standalone comment near the relevant declaration or implementation block:

```rust
// @ref spec/MEDIA.md#5-structural-swaps-the-motivating-contract [implements]
```

Use a repository-root-relative Markdown path, an optional heading fragment,
a required relation, and an optional short gloss following an em dash:

```text
@ref path/to/document.md#heading [relation] — Short explanation
```

| Relation | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `implements` | Implements the referenced requirement |
| `tests` | Exercises the requirement; does not imply exhaustive coverage |
| `constrained-by` | Shaped by an architectural constraint or decision |
| `explains` | Context, not a claim of implementation |
| `historical` | Deliberate reference to retired guidance, not a current constraint |

Normally code/tests point to a **specific spec section**, and that section links
to its ADR. Link directly to an ADR when the architectural boundary itself is
what matters. Use `historical` only for genuine historical context, not to bypass
updating an implementation's governing reference. Proposed ADRs cannot be
implementation constraints until accepted by a maintainer.

Keep directives in source comments (`//`, `///`, `//!`, block-comment `*`, or
`#`), not string literals. References are human-placed breadcrumbs, not
compiler-enforced attachments. The checker validates standalone directive lines;
it does not parse language syntax or prove which declaration a comment governs.
Use normal Markdown links in documentation. This is Pathland's convention,
inspired by LLP, not compatibility with the upstream LLP skill contracts.

## Adoption and change review

- Prioritize non-obvious invariants, architectural boundaries, and behavior an
  agent might otherwise simplify incorrectly. Do not annotate every function.
- Add accurate references when touching governed code; review scope and target
  meaning, not just whether the path exists.
- Requirement changes include spec updates and behavioral tests. Significant
  architectural changes also propose a new ADR, superseding the prior record
  only after maintainer acceptance.
- Keep references, contract changes, tests, and affected `status.md` updates
  together. Do not mechanically annotate files without reviewing their behavior.
- Existing unreferenced code is a review backlog, not an automatic CI failure.

## Drift resolution

Do not assume the code or the document is right merely because it is newer.
Report the discrepancy before changing the governing decision.

| Finding | Resolution |
|---------|------------|
| Code violates a still-valid contract | Fix the implementation and add a regression test |
| Spec misstates intended behavior | Propose a correction and assess compatibility; do not silently bless the code |
| Architecture intentionally changes | Propose a superseding ADR, then coordinate specs, code, and tests |
| Reference is inaccurate or stale | Repair the reference; investigate whether behavior also drifted |
| Intent is uncertain or documents conflict | Record evidence and request a maintainer decision |
| Requirement lacks adequate tests | Record the coverage gap separately from a demonstrated violation |

A finding records: an identifier, audit date and source revision, governing
spec/ADR, implementation symbols, observed behavior, reproduction or test
evidence, existing coverage, and proposed resolution. Distinguish static review,
executed tests, and hypotheses. Never claim a test ran when it did not.

Store cross-project audit reports under `docs/audits/`. Put unresolved
implementation gaps in affected projects' `status.md`, linking to the report;
the audit is evidence, not a competing implementation-status system. Resolve
findings explicitly with a linked fix or a maintainer-approved contract change.
An audit is a dated snapshot, not an automatically current conformance claim.

parts.text:
Now I have complete picture. Let me write the plan.

But before finalizing, let me consider the questions to ask the user. The instruction says ask clarifying questions or opinion when weighing tradeoffs. The user explicitly asked "What decisions do we need to make?" So I should present decision points and recommendations, and ask them to choose on the biggest fork.

I need to be concise but this is a plan; the "fewer than 4 lines" rule is overridden by plan mode and user asking for detail. Still, keep it structured and not bloated.

Let me define the core decision: architecture model.

**Option 1 — Renderer-owned windowing (all rows transmitted)**
- Protocol: add item extent/count hints; renderer realizes visible subset.
- Pros: app code unchanged (just use LazyVStack), renderer-only work; simplest for app authors; matches current spec wording; no new round trips.
- Cons: O(N) app nodes, wire, renderer model memory; ring 4096 slots caps mount (~hundreds of rows) unless chunked/resync; SSR O(N) HTML; doesn't scale to 100k.
- Good for "thousands" if mount is chunked and renderer holds model, but not ideal.

**Option 2 — App-owned windowing (data source + visible-range event)**
- Protocol: lazy container carries `ITEM_COUNT`; renderer reports visible range; app emits only window.
- Pros: O(window) app nodes/wire/renderer; scales to 100k+; true "only visible rendered"; works on all renderers incl. SSR (with viewport + extent).
- Cons: new event + properties; app must provide builder/count; extent/sizing needed for scrollbar; more moving parts; keys/identity; SSR first paint.
- Good for the stated goal.

**Option 3 — Hybrid: renderer requests item content by index from app (renderer-driven pull)**
- Renderer knows count + extent, emits `REQUEST_ITEMS(range)`; app responds with the window. Similar to option 2 but renderer controls window/overscan. More protocol surface and async handshake; not needed if app can window from SCROLL.

Recommendation: Option 2 (app-owned windowing) for scale, with fixed/estimated extent; renderer-side realization can be added later as an optimization. But we should acknowledge that the current spec describes Option 1, so the spec/ADR needs to change.

Wait — but the app-owned model with a window means the renderer must place the window at the right scroll offset. If the app emits a `LazyVStack` containing only window children, the stack naturally packs from the start (scroll offset 0). To preserve scroll extent, either:
- The app emits leading/trailing spacer nodes sized to the missing extent. The app knows `firstIndex`, `itemExtent`, `spacing`, `count`; it can emit a leading `Spacer` with fixed height `firstIndex*(extent+spacing)` and trailing one. But the stack's spacing logic would add gaps around spacers; could compute. This uses existing protocol (fixed HEIGHT on a Color/Spacer). It's doable without new layout semantics, but the app must know extent.
- Or add a `LAZY_RANGE` property (`first index`, `item count`, `item extent`) so the renderer inserts virtual leading/trailing space and positions the window. This is cleaner and keeps the app from emitting spacer nodes. But it introduces a new layout concept: a container with a virtual extent. That's a spec change but a natural one.

Actually, a neat approach: lazy container carries `ITEM_COUNT` + `ITEM_EXTENT` (or `ITEM_EXTENT` absent = measured). App emits the window children plus `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` (u32). Renderer computes:
- total content extent = count*extent + (count-1)*spacing
- window offset = firstIndex*(extent+spacing)
- leading virtual space before the first child = firstIndex*(extent+spacing)
- trailing virtual space = (count - firstIndex - emitted)*...
Then the scroll view sees correct total extent. The renderer reports `SCROLL` offset; the app computes the visible window from offset and emits a new window.

This is basically React Native's VirtualizedList but with the renderer owning the extent math. Or simpler: renderer reports the visible index range directly (it knows offset, viewport, extent, spacing) via a new `VISIBLE_RANGE` event, so the app doesn't duplicate the math. That event is more robust (handles variable extents if renderer measures).

For variable-height rows, `ITEM_EXTENT` can be an estimate; the renderer measures realized rows and adjusts offsets. This is complex. v1: fixed extent per lazy container (uniform row height), which covers many list UIs; variable height later (or app-declared per-index extents list? too big). Another option: `ITEM_EXTENT` absent → renderer measures realized rows and assumes same for unmeasured (estimate). But scroll position drift. Decision needed.

Identity/keys:
- With windowing, the same item index may be recreated at different node ids as the window shifts. That causes TREE delete/create churn (fine for window size ~30) but loses per-row state (e.g. TextField focus, media). Need stable keys or per-index state. The DSL `state()` is component-keyed; if rows are rebuilt, their state resets unless keyed. Decision: add optional keyed identity (`ForEach(items, key = ...)`) or require row state to live in a data model, not component state. Also the emitter reconciles by position+type; a sliding window means all children shift positions → mass delete/create unless the lazy container supports a `FIRST_INDEX` so the renderer maps children to absolute indices and the emitter can preserve ids by index. That's important: node ids stable for same absolute index.

Emitter implication: the app-side retained tree for a windowed lazy container needs to hold only window children, and when the window slides, diff by absolute index (keyed). This is a new emitter feature.

SSR/first paint:
- Server knows viewport only after WS connect, but SSR happens before that (HTTP request has no viewport). Wait: on SSR, the host synthesizes environment from HTTP request: ROUTE only, no viewport. So server can't know viewport at first paint. Options: (a) SSR renders a conservative first window (e.g. first 20 rows) + total extent, client hydrates and resyncs with viewport; (b) use a default viewport; (c) full SSR for SEO/a11y and client virtualizes. Decision needed.
- Actually the DOM client sends viewport on connect and can request RESYNC; so SSR can render first N rows and then client corrects. But SSR HTML must include the virtual extent so scroll works before JS.

Web DOM renderer:
- If app sends only a window, the DOM contains only the window; the scroll container must have virtual extent. Renderer can use padding/margin on the lazy stack, or a spacer div. Fine.
- If we instead renderer-window with all nodes, DOM can use `content-visibility: auto` and skip layout/paint for offscreen, but DOM nodes still exist. Browser-level virtualization via CSS is not "only visible elements".

Native renderers:
- GTK: use `GtkListView`/`GtkColumnView` with `GtkSignalListItemFactory` + `Gio.ListStore` for true recycling; or `GtkBox` + realize/discard. GtkListView requires a model; the protocol's window-of-children can map to a model of realized rows, but recycling needs stable item identity. Qt: `ListView`/`Repeater` with a model; or `ColumnLayout` with manual window.
- Alternatively keep GtkBox/QML ColumnLayout and only create widgets for the window; simpler but not recycling, still fine for window of ~30.

Protocol surface specifics to decide:
- New properties: `ITEM_COUNT` (u32), `ITEM_EXTENT` (f32, main-axis points; maybe per-axis for grids: `ITEM_WIDTH`/`ITEM_HEIGHT`), `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` (u32), maybe `OVERSCAN` (u32 rows) — renderer-owned default? App-declared?
- New event: `VISIBLE_RANGE` (targetId, firstIndex, lastIndex) host→guest, or reuse `SCROLL` and let app compute. Recommend `VISIBLE_RANGE` because it handles measured extents and avoids duplicating layout math in app; also simpler for app authors. But it adds a renderer→app round trip; the renderer can emit it on scroll settle / throttled. Need to define when emitted (after layout/scroll, coalesced).
- Alternatively `SCROLL` already exists and is draft; finish it and add app-side helper. But app would need viewport size and extent; it has neither. So `VISIBLE_RANGE` is better.
- Need listener bit? A lazy container implicitly reports its visible range (like MEDIA_CONTROLLER reports). Or a listener bit (bit 10). Recommend implicit for lazy containers that have `ITEM_COUNT` + window mode; or explicit `EVENT_LISTENERS` bit to keep it opt-in. Decision.

Layout spec:
- Define "virtual extent" for lazy containers: total main-axis size = count*extent + gaps; window children are laid out at their absolute index positions; cross-axis unchanged; Fill/Hug rules; scrollbar extent. This is a real spec addition (LAYOUT/PRIMITIVES).
- Fixed extent only vs measured/estimated.

Emission/ring:
- Even with app windowing, a full snapshot (resync) must emit only the current window + count, not all rows. Good.
- For renderer-owned model, need chunked mount or bigger ring; but with app windowing this goes away.
- Zero-alloc steady state still holds for unchanged window.

Testing:
- Engine traces: window slide delta (remove first row, add last), count change, scroll event → window change.
- Renderer conformance: same visible set given same scroll offset + extent.
- SSR golden: first-window HTML + virtual extent.

Migration/status:
- Update spec/PRIMITIVES (lazy sections), LAYOUT, DSL (ForEach/lazy API), EVENTS (visible range), OPCODE (properties/events), protocol.tsv, constants (Rust/Java/TS), engine, renderers, status.md.
- New ADR: "Virtualized lazy containers" superseding/refining the current renderer-may-defer wording.

Now, the user asked to "plan lazy stacks" and "What do we have so far. What decisions do we need to make?" I should not over-commit to a design without their input. Present the fork and ask.

I should ask maybe 3-4 focused questions:
1. Scaling target: thousands (10k) vs 100k+? Determines whether O(N) app model is acceptable or app-side windowing required.
2. Who owns the window: renderer-side (app unchanged) vs app data-source (new API)?
3. Row sizing: fixed uniform extent v1, or variable-height with estimates?
4. SSR/first paint: window SSR vs full SSR for SEO?
Maybe also: which containers in v1 (VStack first)?

Actually, let me consolidate into a plan with a recommended path and then ask the key questions via the `question` tool? The instructions say use the question tool to ask. But a plan-mode response can just ask in text. The `question` tool is available and good for choices. However, asking multiple complex architecture questions via the tool may be clunky. I could present the analysis, then use the question tool for the top fork. The system says "Ask the user clarifying questions or ask for their opinion when weighing tradeoffs." I'll present the plan and then ask 3 questions using the question tool.

# Lazy stacks: current state & decisions

## What exists today
- Spec: component IDs, allocation identical to eager, "renderer MAY defer realizing" (no mechanism), no item count/extent/range.
- Protocol: no lazy-specific properties/events; SCROLL/WHEEL are draft and not routed to app; viewport environment stored but not exposed to views.
- DSL: LazyVStack etc. build all children eagerly; ForEach eager; no keys.
- Renderers: all treat lazy == eager (HTML CSS flex/grid; GTK GtkBox/GtkGrid; Qt ColumnLayout/Grid; DOM full DOM). No windowing.
- Engine: full tree emitted; ring 4096 slots (~500-1k rows) and 1 MiB arena; Java ring push silently drops when full; SSR FrameOpcodeSink is unbounded but O(N).
- Status: lazy listed as component support, not virtualization.

## Why it doesn't meet the goal
- only native elements could be deferred, but no size model; and app/wire/SSR still O(N).
- 10k rows overflow ring/arena on desktop; O(N) HTML/SSR.

## Decisions
D1. Windowing ownership: renderer-side vs app data-source vs renderer-pull. Recommend app data-source + visible-range event, renderer-owned virtual extent.
D2. Sizing: fixed uniform extent v1; variable-height later (estimate/measure).

D4. Identity: absolute-index stable node ids / keyed rows, so sliding window doesn't churn state; define reconciliation.
D5. SSR/first paint: windowed SSR vs full; how virtual extent is represented in HTML; viewport unavailable at SSR.
D6. Renderer strategy: GTK GtkListView/ColumnView (model recycling) vs realized GtkBox; Qt ListView/Repeater vs ColumnLayout; DOM virtual extent via spacer/padding.
D7. Scope/order: LazyVStack/LazyHStack first, grids second; which platforms first.
D8. Variable-height + scroll anchoring, overscan defaults, and invalidation on data changes.
D9. Conformance/tests + ADR/spec/status updates.

Phase 0: ADR + spec delta.
Phase 1: protocol + engine (count/extent/first index, visible range event, scroll dispatch, viewport exposure), Kotlin/Rust DSL data-source API, emitter keyed window diff.
Phase 2: DOM + HTML SSR virtual extent + window.
Phase 3: GTK/Qt.
Phase 4: variable height/measurement.

1. Scale target & ownership.
2. Fixed vs variable.
3. SSR/SEO stance.

Pathland principle: "Renderers are dumb (execute commands only)", "Applications are Smart (generate commands)", "Only changes matter". App-owned windowing aligns: the app decides which rows to send based on a visible-range event. The renderer only reports raw geometry/scroll (like FIT_CHANGED). This is consistent with `SIZE_THAT_FITS` precedent: renderer measures and reports an index; app swaps children. So app-owned windowing is very much in the spirit.

So recommendation: **App-owned windowing, renderer reports visible range** (precedent: FIT_CHANGED). The lazy container carries `ITEM_COUNT` + `ITEM_EXTENT`; the renderer computes virtual extent and reports `VISIBLE_RANGE`; the app emits the window with `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` so the renderer places it. This is clean and scales.

But is `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` needed if the app emits leading/trailing spacers? Adding FIRST_ITEM_INDEX is cleaner and lets the emitter keep ids stable by absolute index. However, it makes the lazy container's children not start at 0. The renderer must map child i → absolute index first+i. Good.

Alternative to a new `VISIBLE_RANGE` event: expose `SCROLL` + viewport + let app compute. But then app needs extent/spacing math and viewport; more app burden and duplicated layout knowledge. FIT_CHANGED precedent favors a derived event. Recommend `VISIBLE_RANGE` (or `VISIBLE_ITEMS`).

What about overscan? Renderer can include a small overscan and report it, or app adds overscan. Recommend renderer reports the visible range and app applies its own overscan (renderer doesn't need to know). Or a container property `OVERSCAN` (u32) renderer-owned default. Simpler: app adds overscan rows on both sides.

Fixed extent: The container needs an extent to compute the visible range and virtual scroll size before rows are measured. v1 fixed uniform extent. If absent, renderer could measure realized rows and assume uniform; but first frame needs a default. Recommend `ITEM_EXTENT` required for windowing (or `ITEM_EXTENT` = estimated, renderer measures and adjusts).

Grids: `LAZY_VGRID` needs columns; visible range is rows, and items per row = columns; item extent = row height (vertical) / column width (horizontal). For v1, stacks only or include grids with fixed extent.

SSR: Since viewport isn't known at SSR, options:
- Render first K items (e.g. K = 20) + virtual extent via inline height; DOM client hydrates, sends viewport, gets visible range, resyncs window. This gives a correct-looking first paint without knowing viewport.
- For SEO, full list may be desired; but that conflicts with scale. Decision: windowed SSR by default; opt-in full SSR for SEO-critical lists.
Note: The app can also use the viewport environment if the host provides it (e.g. native desktop knows window size; web SSR doesn't). We should expose viewport in Environment for the app to pick an initial window.

Identity: With app-owned window and absolute index, the emitter should key children by absolute index so sliding the window reuses ids for items still in range. This requires a keyed lazy list emitter or assigning ids based on absolute index. But node ids are pre-order and allocated; stable reuse across window slides is a new emitter concern. Could be done by retaining the previous window's nodes and reconciling by absolute index. Worth calling out as a sub-decision. Also, component `state()` for a row would reset when the row leaves the window; recommend row state lives in the data model (or a keyed state scope). This is important for text fields/media.

## What exists today

**Spec surface is already allocated, but only as a naming contract.**

- `LAZY_VGRID 0x15`, `LAZY_HGRID 0x16`, `LAZY_VSTACK 0x1B`, `LAZY_HSTACK 0x1C` (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md:180-185`).
- The lazy sections say allocation is **identical to the eager base** and that a renderer **MAY defer realizing** off-screen children (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md:706-735`; `spec/LAYOUT.md:285`).
- There is **no mechanism** for deferral: no item count, no extent, no visible-range request, no window/offset property. `SCROLL`/`WHEEL` exist only as draft events (`spec/EVENTS.md:248-259`).

**Everything below the spec treats lazy as eager.**

- Kotlin DSL `LazyVStack(...)` builds `childrenOf(content)` immediately (`lib/java/.../dsl/Containers.kt:167`); `ForEach` materializes every row (`lib/java/.../dsl/Views.kt:247`).
- Rust DSL has `LazyVStack`/`LazyHStack`/`LazyVGrid`/`LazyHGrid` structs, but they emit the full child list (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-view/src/lib.rs:2694-2773`).
- GTK maps lazy stacks to `GtkBox` and lazy grids to `GtkGrid` (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/status.md`); Qt maps them to `ColumnLayout`/`RowLayout`/`Grid`; HTML maps them to CSS flex/grid; the DOM client hydrates every node.
- `ForEach` has **no keys** (`spec/DSL.md:1551`), and the emitter reconciles by position + type.

**Scroll/viewport feedback is incomplete.**

- `SCROLL` is decoded but `InputDispatcher` never routes it (`lib/java/.../engine/InputDispatcher.kt:28`), and there is no `onScroll` DSL surface.
- Viewport width/height arrive via `META::ENVIRONMENT` and are stored on the server session (`lib/java/.../PathlandSession.java:281-289`) but are **not exposed to views** (`Environment.kt` has no viewport key).

**The desktop transport cannot carry an eager list anyway.**

- Default ring is **4096 slots (~4095 opcodes)** and **1 MiB arena** (`lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/memory.rs:14-16`). A row is several opcodes, so a mount of thousands of rows overflows.
- Java `RingOpcodeSink.push` **ignores the full-ring return value** (`lib/java/.../nativecore/RingOpcodeSink.kt:114`), so an eager mount can silently drop opcodes and corrupt the tree.
- SSR uses the unbounded `FrameOpcodeSink`, so it “works” but is O(N) in wire bytes, HTML, and browser DOM.

**Net:** we have the component IDs and the “windowed realization” sentence, but no protocol, engine, DSL, or renderer implementation of windowing. Today lazy stacks are cosmetic aliases of eager stacks.

---

## The core gap

The current spec assumes the renderer receives **all children** and chooses which native elements to realize. That is insufficient for the stated goal because:

1. The app still allocates and emits O(N) nodes; the ring/arena cap makes this fail for thousands of rows on desktop.
2. A renderer cannot know the size of an unrealized row, so it cannot compute scroll extent or place the window without a size model.
3. SSR still serializes every row.
4. A sliding window needs stable row identity; position-based reconciliation would delete/recreate rows and lose row-local state.

So we need an explicit virtualization contract, not just a “MAY defer” note.

---

## Decisions we need to make

### D1. Who owns the window? (the big fork)

| Option | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Renderer-owned** | App sends all rows; renderer realizes only visible ones | App API unchanged; closest to current spec wording | O(N) app tree/wire/memory; breaks at ring size; bad SSR; not 100k-scale |
| **B. App-owned data source** | App declares `count` + builder; renderer reports visible range; app emits only that window | O(window) cost; true scale; matches “applications are smart, renderers report measurements” (`FIT_CHANGED` precedent) | New API + event + identity rules; app must handle window updates |
| **C. Renderer pull** | Renderer knows count/extent and requests item ranges from the app | Renderer controls overscan/measurement | Most protocol/async surface; largely redundant with B |

**Recommendation: B**, with the renderer owning the virtual extent math and reporting a visible index range. It is the only option that meets “many thousands without a sweat” and it matches the existing `SIZE_THAT_FITS` pattern (renderer measures → reports → app swaps children).

### D2. Sizing model

- **Fixed uniform extent** per lazy container (e.g. `ITEM_EXTENT = 56pt`) is simple, exact, and gives a correct scrollbar immediately.
- Variable-height needs estimation, measurement caching, and scroll anchoring. It is a meaningful second phase.
- A “measured only” mode cannot size the virtual extent before first realization.

**Recommendation: fixed extent in v1; estimated/measured later.**

### D3. Protocol additions

Likely:
- Container properties: `ITEM_COUNT` (u32), `ITEM_EXTENT` (f32 main-axis points; grids need per-axis extent), `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` (u32) to place the emitted window, possibly `OVERSCAN`.
- Host→guest event: `VISIBLE_RANGE` (targetId, firstIndex, lastIndex) — or finish `SCROLL` + expose viewport and make the app compute the range.
- Decide whether a lazy container implicitly reports its range (like `MEDIA_CONTROLLER`) or requires a listener bit.

**Recommendation: `VISIBLE_RANGE` (derived, like `FIT_CHANGED`), `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` on the container, fixed `ITEM_EXTENT`; app applies overscan.**

### D4. Identity and reconciliation

- Children of a windowed lazy container should map to **absolute indices**, so sliding the window reuses node ids for rows still visible.
- Define keyed rows or index-stable slots; row-local `state()` must not silently reset when a row leaves/re-enters the window.
- Decide whether row state lives in the data model or in a keyed state scope.

### D5. SSR / first paint / SEO

- Web SSR does **not** know viewport height at render time (only `ROUTE` is synthesized from the HTTP request; viewport arrives later over WS).
- Options: render a conservative first window (e.g. 20 rows) plus the virtual extent, then let the client resync; or full SSR for SEO/a11y-critical lists; or make windowed SSR opt-in.

**Recommendation: windowed SSR first window + correct virtual extent; opt-in full SSR for SEO-critical lists.**

### D6. Renderer strategy per platform

- **DOM/HTML:** virtual extent via spacer/padding on the lazy container; only window children in the DOM. (Could use `content-visibility: auto` as an interim mitigation, but that is not true virtualization.)
- **GTK4:** `GtkListView`/`GtkColumnView` + `Gio.ListStore` + factory for true recycling, or realized `GtkBox` for a simpler v1.
- **Qt Quick:** `ListView`/`Repeater` with a model, or `ColumnLayout` with a realized window.

Decide whether v1 recycles native elements or only avoids creating off-screen ones.

### D7. Scope and phasing

- v1: `LazyVStack`/`LazyHStack` only, or include grids?
- Which platforms first (DOM + SSR are easiest to validate; GTK/Qt after).
- What happens to the existing eager `ForEach` (keep for small lists; lazy API separate).

### D8. Invalidation

- Data insert/remove changes `count` and shifts indices; define whether the window is re-requested, how ids are preserved, and how scroll anchoring works.
- Define behavior when `count` changes while scrolled.

### D9. Conformance and governance

- New ADR (the current “renderer MAY defer” wording is not enough and will be superseded/refined).
- Spec updates: `PRIMITIVES.md`, `LAYOUT.md`, `DSL.md`, `EVENTS.md`, `OPCODE.md`, `protocol.tsv`.
- Rust/Java/TS constants, engine, DSL, renderers, and `status.md`.
- Engine traces for window slide, count change, and visible-range handling; renderer conformance for “same scroll offset + extent → same visible set.”

---

## Suggested phased plan

1. **ADR + spec delta**: decide D1/D2/D3, define virtual extent and window semantics.
2. **Protocol + core**: constants, manifest, `VISIBLE_RANGE`, `ITEM_COUNT`/`ITEM_EXTENT`/`FIRST_ITEM_INDEX`, viewport exposure, finish `SCROLL` dispatch.
3. **Engine + Kotlin/Rust DSL**: data-source lazy list API, window diff, absolute-index identity.
4. **DOM + HTML SSR**: virtual extent, window hydration, first-window SSR.
5. **GTK/Qt**: realized window first, native recycling second.
6. **Variable height** and measurement.

- `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX` (u32) — absolute index of the first emitted child.
- `OVERSCAN`? Decide app-side. Renderer reports exact visible range; app adds overscan. No protocol property needed.
- Maybe `ITEM_SPACING`? Existing `SPACING` already used between children. But virtual extent needs the gap between all items, including across the window boundary. Use `SPACING` for both; compute total = count*extent + (count-1)*spacing.
- For horizontal lazy stack, extent is width.

Event:
- `VISIBLE_RANGE` (host→guest), A=targetId (the lazy container), B=firstIndex (u32), C=lastIndexExclusive (u32) or (first,count). Use B=first, C=count. Recommendation: implicit (like media), because without it the container can't function. But the renderer needs to know which lazy container is inside a scroll viewport. The lazy container itself is the target; renderer computes intersection with the nearest scroll ancestor's viewport.

Also expose `VIEWPORT_WIDTH/HEIGHT` to the app Environment (for initial window choice). The renderer/server already has it. Add `Platform.VIEWPORT` or `Environment` key. ### Layout semantics (spec)

- A lazy stack with `ITEM_COUNT` + `ITEM_EXTENT` has a **virtual main-axis extent**:
  `contentExtent = ITEM_COUNT * ITEM_EXTENT + max(0, ITEM_COUNT - 1) * SPACING`.
- The container lays out only its emitted children; child `i` is placed at absolute index `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX + i`, at offset `index * (ITEM_EXTENT + SPACING)`.

- Children are exactly `ITEM_EXTENT` on the main axis (the container sets it; app need not). Cross-axis per normal stack alignment.
- When `ITEM_COUNT`/`ITEM_EXTENT` absent, the lazy stack behaves exactly like the eager stack (backward compatible).

- Define what happens if the emitted window doesn't cover the visible range (renderer shows blank/placeholder? It should report the range; app is expected to respond). Decide: renderer reports and does not invent rows.

  - The app stores a `WritableSignal<IntRange>` (visible window) updated by the `VISIBLE_RANGE` input.
  - The emitter renders only the window's rows, setting `FIRST_ITEM_INDEX`.
  - Node ids: reconcile by absolute index. Actually, the engine traces are emitted from the Rust engine (`pathland-engine-golden`). If we add new emission behavior, we should implement it in Rust first to emit traces, then Java must match. So plan: Rust engine + Java emitter together.

**DOM/HTML:**
- HTML renders the lazy container with a wrapper that has a **main-axis virtual extent** (e.g. `height: contentExtent px` for vertical) and positions the window children at `firstIndex*(extent+spacing)` using padding-top or absolute positioning.
